# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

# SMA-834: Anthropic translator keeps an open tool round whole at a tool-use-only assistant message

## Intent

The core model has two equal forms for a tool call: a top-level
`Item::ToolCall`, and a `ContentPart::ToolUse` nested inside an
`Item::AssistantMessage`. In
`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/translate/request.rs` the two
forms give different wire orders inside an open tool round. The nested form
splits the round, and the Anthropic API rejects the request because a user turn
lacks a `tool_result` for a `tool_use` in the turn before it.

SMA-824 (PR #365, commit `4a0f832b`) fixed the same gap in the Bedrock
translator. This change ports that rule.

## Current behavior

- The `ToolCall` arm keeps the pending results when `round_is_answered` is
  `false`. It appends its `tool_use` block to the last assistant message in
  `messages` (or to `pending_tool_use` when the last message is not an
  assistant message).
- The `AssistantMessage` arm, for a non-empty message, always flushes
  `pending_tool_use` and `pending_tool_results`, then pushes a new assistant
  message.

Example items: `user q, assistant[ToolUse t1, ToolUse t2], ToolResult t1,
assistant[ToolUse t3], ToolResult t2, ToolResult t3`.

- Today: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2], user[r1], assistant[t3], user[r2, r3]`.
  This is invalid.
- With the fix: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2, t3], user[r1, r2, r3]`. This is the
  same wire as the `Item::ToolCall t3` form.

## Goals

- A non-empty `AssistantMessage` joins the open round when all three conditions
  are true:
  1. every block in it is a `tool_use` block,
  2. `pending_tool_results` is not empty,
  3. `round_is_answered(&messages, &pending_tool_results)` is `false`.
- "Joins" means the same thing as in the `ToolCall` arm: the pending results stay
  pending, and the blocks go to the end of the last assistant message in
  `messages`. If the last message is not an assistant message, the blocks go to
  `pending_tool_use`. (When the round is not answered, the last message is
  always an assistant message, because `round_is_answered` returns `true` for an
  empty trailing assistant run. The fallback only keeps the code total.)
- `last_item_dropped` becomes `false` on that path, as for any kept message.

## Non-goals

- No change for a message with text and tool uses, an answered round, no
  pending results, or an empty message. These keep their current behavior.
- No change to `round_is_answered`, to `user_blocks`, or to `assistant_blocks`.
- No change to other providers. Bedrock is already fixed. Other translators are
  out of scope for this issue.

## Anti-goals

- No change to the wire for a well-formed request. The existing tests stay green
  without edits, including `round_spanning_adjacent_assistant_messages_is_not_split`
  (two adjacent nested messages with no pending results stay two messages).

## Approaches

1. **Port the Bedrock condition into the `AssistantMessage` arm (chosen).** One
   extra branch before the current flush. It matches Bedrock and the `ToolCall`
   arm, and it is the smallest change.
2. **Turn a tool-use-only message into `Item::ToolCall` items and reuse that
   arm.** This duplicates the arm's logic through a refactor of the loop for no
   gain, and it makes the two translators differ in shape.
3. **Merge every tool-use-only message into the previous assistant message.**
   This changes the wire for well-formed requests (for example, two adjacent
   nested messages), so it breaks the anti-goal.

## Tests

Unit tests in the `tests` module of `request.rs`, with Anthropic wire arrays:

- `nested_tool_use_inside_open_round_joins_it`: the example above gives
  `[utext("q"), assistant[tu(t1), tu(t2), tu(t3)], user[tr(t1), tr(t2), tr(t3)]]`.
- `nested_tool_use_after_answered_round_starts_new_round`:
  `user q, assistant[t1], ToolResult t1, assistant[t2], ToolResult t2` gives
  `[utext("q"), assistant[tu(t1)], user[tr(t1)], assistant[tu(t2)], user[tr(t2)]]`.

Builder's call: also add one test for a mixed message (text plus tool use)
inside an open round, to lock in that it keeps the current flush behavior.

## Docs

Internal translation fix. The public API, the mdBook, and the crate README do
not change.

  ## Verdict: APPROVE WITH CHANGES
  The fix is correct, and the port fits the Anthropic structure. I found no input where a request that the API accepts today changes. The required changes are about the test plan and about writing down the rules that make the port safe.
  
  ## Findings
  
  ### BLOCKER
  None.
  
  ### MAJOR
  - **The mixed-message test, as written in the spec, asserts a request that the API rejects. It is also the only test for condition 1.**
    - **What is wrong:** Take `user q, asst[t1, t2], r1, asst[text b, tu t3], r2, r3`. The current flush gives `asst[t1, t2], user[r1], asst[b, t3], user[r2, r3]`. The user turn after `asst[t1, t2]` has no result for `t2`, so Anthropic returns a 400. A test that asserts this array as "expected" makes a known-bad request look intended. But no existing test in `request.rs` or `mod.rs` sends a non-empty text assistant message inside an open round. So if a builder removes condition 1 ("every block is `tool_use`"), every test stays green. "Builder's call" thus leaves two bad results: no test for condition 1, or a test that asserts a 400.
    - **Why it matters:** The next engineer reads the test as the contract. Or condition 1 has no test at all.
    - **Suggested fix:**
      1. Make the test required, and write it as a parity test. Translate the nested form `asst[text b, tu t3]` and the top-level form `asst(text b), ToolCall t3`, and assert that the two outputs are equal. `build_items` (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:510`) emits exactly this top-level form for a response with text and calls. Both forms flush today, so the test asserts the parity that condition 1 exists for, not one specific request.
      2. Add a doc comment that says both forms still give a rejected request.
      3. List "a text-only or mixed message inside an open round" in Non-goals as a known gap.
      4. File one Linear follow-up for Anthropic and Bedrock. Bedrock's `assistant_message_flushes_calls_before_results` asserts the same shape for a text-only message. I expect Converse to reject it by the same rule, but I did not see a probe for it.
  
  ### MINOR
  - **Say that condition 1 is checked on the output of `assistant_blocks`.** "Every block in it is a `tool_use` block" can also be read as "every `ContentPart` is a `ToolUse`". The two readings differ for `[Reasoning, ToolUse t3]` and `[Text " ", ToolUse t3]`. With the raw-parts reading, these messages do not join, and the request stays a 400. Bedrock checks the filtered blocks (`bedrock/src/translate/request.rs:212`). Suggested fix: write "after `assistant_blocks` drops blank text, reasoning and unsupported parts". Add one test with `[Reasoning, ToolUse t3]` inside an open round. A caller that stores responses from a thinking model in the nested form makes this shape.
  - **Add a test where the join goes into a run of adjacent assistant messages.** Both proposed tests have only one assistant message in the open round. No test shows that the join goes to the last message of a run with more than one message. Suggested fix: copy `round_spanning_adjacent_assistant_messages_is_not_split` and replace `call("t3")` with a nested `t3`. The expected array does not change. The test then also shows parity between the forms.
  - **Write down the second invariant that makes "append to the last message" correct.** The spec says that on the join path the last message is an assistant message. The port also needs `pending_tool_use` to be empty on that path. If it were not empty, the joined blocks would go before the queued calls. The invariant is true:
    - `pending_tool_use` gets blocks only when the last message is not an assistant message.
    - Every `ToolResult` flushes `pending_tool_use` first.
    - So when results are pending, `pending_tool_use` is empty.
  
    Suggested fix: state this rule in the spec and in the code comment.
  - **The fallback is dead code.** On the join path the last message is always an assistant message, so a copied `else { pending_tool_use.extend(..) }` never runs. No test can cover it. If it ran, it would put the calls in a new assistant turn before the user turn with the pending results. Suggested fix: move "append to the last assistant message, else queue" into one helper. Call it from the `ToolCall` arm and from the new branch. The `ToolCall` tests then cover the fallback, and the two arms cannot become different.
  - **Setting `last_item_dropped = false` does nothing on this path.**
    - The flag becomes `true` only when a `UserMessage` gives no blocks.
    - That message takes all the pending results, so after it no results are pending.
    - Results can become pending again only through a `ToolResult`, and a `ToolResult` sets the flag to `false`.
    - So on the join path the flag is already `false`, and `trailing_message_dropped` cannot change.
  
    Suggested fix: keep the line for symmetry. Say in the spec that no test can observe it, so that no reviewer asks for one.
  - **State the assumption behind the join.** The join assumes that an assistant message inside an open round belongs to the same model response. The API cannot answer partial results, so this is usually true. But in a log where a result was written late (for example `r2` after `t3`), the fix now sends a valid request in a different order instead of getting a 400. The `ToolCall` arm already accepts this trade-off (`interleaved_parallel_round_is_not_split`). Suggested fix: write the assumption in Goals.
  - **Say that duplicate ids are not removed.** For `asst[t1, t2], r1, asst[tu t1]`, the join gives `asst[t1, t2, t1]`, and the API rejects the duplicate id.   - **Add a live test.** SMA-819 recorded live probes and `#[ignore]` live tests for each claim about the wire format. This spec makes such a claim but has only unit tests. The fixed shape is the normal parallel tool shape, so the risk is low. Suggested fix: add `nested_tool_use_inside_open_round_is_accepted` to `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/tests/live.rs`. Use `run_accepted` and ids in the `toolu_...` form, and record a real run in the PR.
  - **Fix the references and the doc scope.**
    - The spec cites commit `4a0f832b` for PR #365. I could not confirm that SHA. The squash commit on `main` is `4003a131`, and a branch commit can become unreachable after the branch is deleted.
    - Add the SMA-834 Linear link, as the other specs do.
    - The Docs section should include the code comment of the `AssistantMessage` arm. That comment must explain the new branch, as Bedrock's comment does at lines 206-210.
  
  ### QUESTIONS
  - Did a live probe test a round that spans adjacent assistant messages? Probe P4 in SMA-819 shows that the API joins adjacent text-only assistant turns. I found no probe that shows a `tool_use` in an earlier adjacent message matched by a `tool_result` after the later one (`asst[tu t1], asst[tu t2], user[r1, r2]`). The existing `round_spanning_adjacent_assistant_messages_is_not_split` depends on this, and so does the test I suggest above.

  - Should a text-only or mixed message inside an open round join the round in the future? That would give a valid request. But it keeps parity only if the top-level `AssistantMessage(text)` path in Anthropic and Bedrock changes as well. Decide this in the follow-up, not in this ticket.

  - The three conditions are the right gate, and condition 2 is necessary. The new branch runs only when today's output already has a user turn without a result for a `tool_use` in the turn before it. So no request that the API accepts today changes, and the anti-goal holds. I traced every existing test, including `tests/messages_streaming.rs`, and none of them reaches the new branch.

I checked every item type that can follow a join (`ToolResult`, `UserMessage`, `System`, an assistant message with only tool uses or with text, `ToolCall`, end of input). Each gives the same request in both translators, because the round stays open until the next `ToolResult`. In Anthropic the joined blocks are also visible to later `round_is_answered` checks right away.

# SMA-834: Anthropic translator keeps an open tool round whole at a tool-use-only assistant message

Linear: [SMA-834](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-834/anthropic-translator-splits-an-open-tool-round-at-a-tool-use-only)

## Intent

The core model has two equal forms for a tool call: a top-level
`Item::ToolCall`, and a `ContentPart::ToolUse` nested inside an
`Item::AssistantMessage`. In
`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/translate/request.rs` the two
forms give different wire orders inside an open tool round. The nested form
splits the round, and the Anthropic API rejects the request because a user turn
lacks a `tool_result` for a `tool_use` in the turn before it.

SMA-824 fixed the same gap in the Bedrock translator (PR #365, squash commit
`4003a131` on `main`). This change ports that rule.

## Current behavior

- The `ToolCall` arm keeps the pending results when `round_is_answered` is
  `false`. It appends its `tool_use` block to the last assistant message in
  `messages`, or to `pending_tool_use` when the last message is not an
  assistant message.
- The `AssistantMessage` arm, for a non-empty message, always flushes
  `pending_tool_use` and `pending_tool_results`, then pushes a new assistant
  message.

Example items: `user q, assistant[ToolUse t1, ToolUse t2], ToolResult t1,
assistant[ToolUse t3], ToolResult t2, ToolResult t3`.

- Today: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2], user[r1], assistant[t3], user[r2, r3]`.
  The API rejects this.
- With the fix: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2, t3], user[r1, r2, r3]`. This is the
  same wire as the `Item::ToolCall t3` form.

## Goals

- A non-empty `AssistantMessage` joins the open round when all three conditions
  are true:
  1. every block in the **output of `assistant_blocks`** is a `tool_use` block.
     `assistant_blocks` already drops blank text, reasoning, and unsupported
     parts, so `[Reasoning, ToolUse t3]` and `[Text " ", ToolUse t3]` join.
     This matches Bedrock.
  2. `pending_tool_results` is not empty,
  3. `round_is_answered(&messages, &pending_tool_results)` is `false`.
- "Joins" means the same thing as in the `ToolCall` arm: the pending results stay
  pending, and the blocks go to the end of the last assistant message in
  `messages`. One private helper does "append to the last assistant message, or
  else queue in `pending_tool_use`". The `ToolCall` arm and the new branch both
  call it, so the two paths cannot become different.
- Two invariants make the append correct. The code comment states both:
  - On the join path the last message is an assistant message.
    `round_is_answered` returns `true` for an empty trailing assistant run, so
    condition 3 needs at least one assistant message at the end.
  - On the join path `pending_tool_use` is empty. It gets blocks only when the
    last message is not an assistant message, and each `ToolResult` flushes it.
    Condition 2 needs a `ToolResult` after the last queue.
- `last_item_dropped` becomes `false` on that path, for symmetry with every
  kept message. No test can observe it: on the join path the flag is already
  `false`, because a `ToolResult` came after any dropped user message.
- Assumption: an assistant message inside an open round belongs to the same
  model response. The `ToolCall` arm already makes this assumption
  (`interleaved_parallel_round_is_not_split`). For a log with a late result,
  the fix sends a valid request in a different order instead of a rejected one.

## Non-goals

- No change for an answered round, for no pending results, or for an empty
  message. These keep their current behavior.
- **Known gap, kept as is:** a text-only or mixed (text plus tool use) assistant
  message inside an open round still flushes. The nested form and the
  top-level form (`AssistantMessage(text)` then `ToolCall`, as `build_items`
  emits) both give a request that the API rejects. Bedrock has the same gap
  (`assistant_message_flushes_calls_before_results`). This goes to a follow-up
  issue for both translators.
- No de-duplication of tool-use ids. `asst[t1, t2], r1, asst[tu t1]` gives
  `asst[t1, t2, t1]`, which the API rejects. Today's output is also rejected,
  and the `ToolCall` arm does not de-duplicate either.
- No change to `round_is_answered`, `user_blocks`, or `assistant_blocks`.

`Item::ToolCall`, and a `ContentPart::ToolUse` nested inside an
`Item::AssistantMessage`. In

forms give different wire orders inside an open tool round. The nested form
splits the round, and the Anthropic API rejects the request because a user turn
lacks a `tool_result` for a `tool_use` in the turn before it.

SMA-824 fixed the same gap in the Bedrock translator (PR #365, squash commit
`4003a131` on `main`). This change ports that rule.

## Current behavior

- The `ToolCall` arm keeps the pending results when `round_is_answered` is
  `false`. It appends its `tool_use` block to the last assistant message in
  `messages`, or to `pending_tool_use` when the last message is not an
  assistant message.
- The `AssistantMessage` arm, for a non-empty message, always flushes
  `pending_tool_use` and `pending_tool_results`, then pushes a new assistant
  message.

Example items: `user q, assistant[ToolUse t1, ToolUse t2], ToolResult t1,
assistant[ToolUse t3], ToolResult t2, ToolResult t3`.

  same wire as the `Item::ToolCall t3` form.

  are true:

     parts, so `[Reasoning, ToolUse t3]` and `[Text " ", ToolUse t3]` join.

# SMA-834: Anthropic translator keeps an open tool round whole at a tool-use-only assistant message

## Intent

The core model has two equal forms for a tool call: a top-level
`Item::ToolCall`, and a `ContentPart::ToolUse` nested inside an
`Item::AssistantMessage`. In
`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/translate/request.rs` the two
forms give different wire orders inside an open tool round. The nested form
splits the round, and the Anthropic API rejects the request because a user turn
lacks a `tool_result` for a `tool_use` in the turn before it.

SMA-824 (PR #365, commit `4a0f832b`) fixed the same gap in the Bedrock
translator. This change ports that rule.

## Current behavior

- The `ToolCall` arm keeps the pending results when `round_is_answered` is
  `false`. It appends its `tool_use` block to the last assistant message in
  `messages` (or to `pending_tool_use` when the last message is not an
  assistant message).
- The `AssistantMessage` arm, for a non-empty message, always flushes
  `pending_tool_use` and `pending_tool_results`, then pushes a new assistant
  message.

Example items: `user q, assistant[ToolUse t1, ToolUse t2], ToolResult t1,
assistant[ToolUse t3], ToolResult t2, ToolResult t3`.

- Today: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2], user[r1], assistant[t3], user[r2, r3]`.
  This is invalid.
- With the fix: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2, t3], user[r1, r2, r3]`. This is the
  same wire as the `Item::ToolCall t3` form.

## Goals

- A non-empty `AssistantMessage` joins the open round when all three conditions
  are true:
  1. every block in it is a `tool_use` block,
  2. `pending_tool_results` is not empty,
  3. `round_is_answered(&messages, &pending_tool_results)` is `false`.
- "Joins" means the same thing as in the `ToolCall` arm: the pending results stay
  pending, and the blocks go to the end of the last assistant message in
  `messages`. If the last message is not an assistant message, the blocks go to
  `pending_tool_use`. (When the round is not answered, the last message is
  always an assistant message, because `round_is_answered` returns `true` for an
  empty trailing assistant run. The fallback only keeps the code total.)
- `last_item_dropped` becomes `false` on that path, as for any kept message.

## Non-goals

- No change for a message with text and tool uses, an answered round, no
  pending results, or an empty message. These keep their current behavior.
- No change to `round_is_answered`, to `user_blocks`, or to `assistant_blocks`.
- No change to other providers. Bedrock is already fixed. Other translators are
  out of scope for this issue.

## Anti-goals

- No change to the wire for a well-formed request. The existing tests stay green
  without edits, including `round_spanning_adjacent_assistant_messages_is_not_split`
  (two adjacent nested messages with no pending results stay two messages).

## Approaches

1. **Port the Bedrock condition into the `AssistantMessage` arm (chosen).** One
   extra branch before the current flush. It matches Bedrock and the `ToolCall`
   arm, and it is the smallest change.
2. **Turn a tool-use-only message into `Item::ToolCall` items and reuse that
   arm.** This duplicates the arm's logic through a refactor of the loop for no
   gain, and it makes the two translators differ in shape.
3. **Merge every tool-use-only message into the previous assistant message.**
   This changes the wire for well-formed requests (for example, two adjacent
   nested messages), so it breaks the anti-goal.

## Tests

Unit tests in the `tests` module of `request.rs`, with Anthropic wire arrays:

- `nested_tool_use_inside_open_round_joins_it`: the example above gives
  `[utext("q"), assistant[tu(t1), tu(t2), tu(t3)], user[tr(t1), tr(t2), tr(t3)]]`.
- `nested_tool_use_after_answered_round_starts_new_round`:
  `user q, assistant[t1], ToolResult t1, assistant[t2], ToolResult t2` gives
  `[utext("q"), assistant[tu(t1)], user[tr(t1)], assistant[tu(t2)], user[tr(t2)]]`.

Builder's call: also add one test for a mixed message (text plus tool use)
inside an open round, to lock in that it keeps the current flush behavior.

## Docs

Internal translation fix. The public API, the mdBook, and the crate README do
not change.

## Gate 1: spec approval

**Spec:** `/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-824/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-20-anthropic-open-round-nested-tool-use-design.md`

**The fix:** A non-empty assistant message can join an open tool round, as an `Item::ToolCall` does. It joins only when three things are true:
- All of its blocks are tool uses, counted after the translator removes blank text and reasoning.
- Tool results are pending.
- The round is not answered.

One helper does the append for both paths, so the two paths cannot drift apart. A request that the API accepts today does not change.

**Challenger verdict: APPROVE WITH CHANGES.** It found no blockers. It traced every existing test, and none of them reaches the new branch.

**Changes I made to the spec:**
- **MAJOR, fixed:** My earlier plan for a mixed-message test (text plus tool use) asserted a request that the API rejects. I changed it to a parity test. The nested form and the top-level form must give equal output. This is now the only test that fails if someone removes the "only tool uses" condition. The mixed case is listed as a known gap that this change does not fix.
- **Rule made explicit:** The "only tool uses" check runs after blank text and reasoning are removed, as in Bedrock. A new test covers `[Reasoning, ToolUse]`.
- **New test:** A test now covers a join into a run of more than one adjacent assistant message.
- **Code comment:** The comment states two rules that make the append correct: the last message is an assistant message, and the queue of pending tool uses is empty.
- **Fallback:** The fallback path that a copy would leave as dead code goes into the shared helper.
- **Written down:**
  - Setting the "last message dropped" flag has no effect that a test can see.
  - The join assumes the message belongs to the same model response.
  - Duplicate tool-use ids are not removed.
- **Live test:** I added an `#[ignore]` live test.
- **References:** The spec now cites the squash commit `4003a131` and has the Linear link.

**Rejected:** None. Two of the challenger's questions stay open, and I did not act on them:
- No live probe shows yet that the API accepts a round over adjacent assistant messages. The new live test can check this if an API key is available.
- I did not check whether the OpenAI, LiteLLM, and Gemini translators have the same gap. They are out of scope.

**Decisions for you:**
1. Do you approve the spec?
2. Do you want me to file a Linear follow-up for the known gap? The gap is a text-only or mixed assistant message inside an open round, in both Anthropic and Bedrock.

**Release PR #361 (not part of this work):** All of its CI checks passed. But GitHub reports it as `CONFLICTING` with `main` since PR #365 merged. Release-plz usually makes the PR again on the next run. If it stays in conflict, it needs a look before you merge it.

input.title: Anthropic and Bedrock translators split an open tool round at a text or mixed assistant message
input.description:
Inside an open tool round (results pending, not all calls answered), an assistant message with text flushes the pending results. This is true for a text-only message and for a mixed message (text plus tool use). The flush puts a user turn that lacks some results right after the open assistant turn, so the API rejects the request.

Both forms of the core model give the same rejected request:

* Nested: `AssistantMessage[Text b, ToolUse t3]`.
* Top-level: `AssistantMessage[Text b]`, then `ToolCall t3`. This is the form that `build_items` emits for a response with text and calls.

## Example

Items: `user q, assistant[t1, t2], ToolResult t1, assistant[text b, tool use t3], ToolResult t2, ToolResult t3`

Wire today: `user[q], assistant[t1, t2], user[r1], assistant[b, t3], user[r2, r3]`. The user turn after `assistant[t1, t2]` has no result for `t2`.

## Scope

* Anthropic: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/src/translate/request.rs`, the `AssistantMessage` arm. The parity test `mixed_assistant_inside_open_round_matches_top_level_form` (added for SMA-834) records the current behavior.
* Bedrock: `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-bedrock/src/translate/request.rs`. The test `assistant_message_flushes_calls_before_results` asserts the same shape for a text-only message.

## Open questions

* Should a text or mixed message inside an open round join the round? That gives a valid request. Parity between the two forms needs the top-level `AssistantMessage(text)` path to change in both translators too.
* Bedrock Converse probably rejects this shape by the same rule. No live probe confirms it yet.

Found by the spec challenge for SMA-834.
